title: Tell me about a time you disagreed with another engineer.
description: Learn how to answer the engineering disagreement interview question. Covers how to show constructive conflict resolution, what signals you should send, and how to avoid common traps.

data.text: This question is about how you behave when you are not the only smart person in the room. Interviewers want to know if you can argue for what you believe in, listen to opposing arguments, and reach a better outcome than either person could have reached alone. The right answer shows technical maturity and emotional intelligence in equal measure.
What Makes a Good Disagreement Story

A good disagreement story has three elements: a real technical tension, a process for resolving it, and a shared outcome. The tension should be genuine — do not tell a story where you were right and the other engineer was obviously wrong. The process should show that you treated the other person as a peer, not an obstacle. The outcome should be something better than what either of you started with.

items: Real technical tension: Both sides had reasonable arguments
Respectful process: You discussed, gathered data, or escalated to a standard
Better outcome: The resolution incorporated insights from both sides
Preserved relationship: You continued to work together effectively afterward

data.text: Set up the disagreement clearly, explain both positions fairly, describe how you worked toward a resolution, and share the outcome. The key is to represent the other engineer's argument accurately — interviewers can tell when you are caricaturing the opposing view to make your own position look better.

items: The context: What you were building and why the disagreement arose
Both positions: State the other engineer's view fairly before explaining yours
The process: How you discussed it — data, prototypes, RFC, or escalation to a shared standard
The outcome: What you decided and why it was better than either original position
The relationship: How you continued working together after the disagreement

data.text: A common type of disagreement is API design. One engineer wants a RESTful approach; another prefers GraphQL or event-driven design. Both positions are defensible, and the best choice depends on the client needs, the team's operational experience, and the long-term maintenance cost.

data.title: Sample Answer Outline
data.content:
I was working on a new customer data API with another senior engineer. I advocated for a REST API with versioned endpoints because our clients were primarily server-side services that were already consuming REST APIs. My colleague wanted a GraphQL API because it would let clients request only the data they needed, reducing bandwidth for mobile clients.

Both positions were reasonable. I had built and operated REST APIs at scale; my colleague had seen GraphQL reduce payload sizes significantly in a previous role. Rather than argue from experience alone, we agreed to write a short RFC comparing the two approaches on criteria we both cared about: client flexibility, operational simplicity, performance, and migration cost.

We presented the RFC to the team. The data showed that our mobile clients would benefit from GraphQL, but our server-side services would not. We decided to build the core data layer as REST and expose a GraphQL gateway in front of it. This gave mobile clients the flexibility they needed while keeping the backend simpler for internal services.

The outcome was better than either original position. The RFC process also became our standard for future API design decisions. My colleague and I continued to collaborate on the project, and the gateway approach performed well in production.

data.text: Interviewers want to see that you can hold a strong opinion lightly — that you argue for your view but are willing to change it when presented with better evidence. They also want to know if you make the disagreement about people or about ideas. An answer that paints the other engineer as stubborn or uninformed is a red flag, even if you were technically correct.

terms.definition: Advocating firmly for your position while remaining open to better evidence
Representing the opposing argument in its strongest form before responding to it
An agreed-upon criterion or process for breaking a tie, such as data, an RFC, or an architecture review board

data.title: Common Pitfall
data.text: Do not tell a story where you convinced the other engineer they were wrong. Interviewers prefer stories where both sides contributed to a better outcome. Winning an argument is not the signal — building something better together is.

Some of the best disagreement stories are the ones where you were wrong. If you can describe a disagreement where you started with one position, listened to the other engineer, and changed your mind based on something they said, that signals intellectual humility and strong collaboration skills. These stories are often more memorable than stories where you were right all along.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Represent the other engineer's view fairly — accuracy here signals maturity
Show that the resolution was better than either original position
Preserve the relationship: explain how you worked together afterward
Stories where you changed your mind are powerful signals of humility
Avoid framing the other person as wrong; frame the process as collaborative
